entry.title: Happy Hacking New Year, 2027 Edition
entry.content:
Inspiration

Once I was just looking for something on my computer and saw this:

It's a documentation browser, and it looks outdated, because it's written in Perl and old Tk, but it accomplishes a lot:

  • It can open documentation in pdf, dvi, ps, txt and html formats
  • It has a search
  • It can print
  • It has games!
  • It has Settings and About sections

The authors were probably concerned about simplicity, size, speed and some other stuff which modern developers do not remember how to spell. And I thought: it's a perfect candidate to do something, as the content (still useful, by the way) is there. Maybe someone even wrote something more modern, but it will not stop us!

The ways

According to what I've learned and bearing portability in mind, there are the following paths to improve the user experience and worsen everything else, he-he-he:

  • Zenity, if you prefer pure shell scripting – and it's probably a good path here, because you're going to call external programs a lot
  • Python + Tk, if you prefer Python (which is not a bad idea per se, but do not forget the linter)
  • Go + Tk, which is the closest to the original idea you can get and even one step further (as Go is a lot better than Perl)
  • An HTML page with a search or a number of HTML pages, which you'll probably want to generate programmatically
  • .net with avalonia, just don't think about the app size so much
  • A web app would probably be overkill, but nevertheless: a web app
  • And, new in our list: a local LLM with a vector database to ask questions about the docs and get the answers

Conclusion

Programming by hand and not generating code seems counter-intuitive, but I'd argue that it's still one of the most satisfying hobbies, especially when you do understand what each line of code and each function does and why it's written this way. That doesn't mean you can't ask for clarifications, examples, directions, but don't rob yourself of pure joy, creating something new and useful, which works just like you designed it.

entry.title: Life Is Harder, Make No Mistake
entry.content:
Intro

I've read some stories online about young people facing anxiety and disappointment for different reasons, starting from the climate change, conflicts, future uncertainty in general and ending with a frustrating job search experiences. My personal take on this: life did become harder in many aspects, and you are not exaggerating, overreacting or hallucinating. What's happening is the race for power and resources, and it's not humane in any way. I've seen people successfully evading reality, and there are a lot of places in this world where you can do that without any substances, where history has just stopped, but I don't think it's the way out. My answer is to face reality and deal with it. And this post is a short description of how I do it.

Wars

The war in Ukraine affected me directly, so I heard a lot of opinions from Russians and Ukrainians, as well as listened to analytical podcasts trying to point out the reasons for what's going on. And there was one phrase that made it clear to me: soldiers pay for the mistakes of politicians. As I understand it, not being a politician myself, the whole point of politics is to prevent wars and to build a peace architecture. So you have wars when politics and politicians have failed. And when you unleash the war dogs, you don't manage the situation anymore, you expect the outcome.

Next, I believe humans can deal with a finite amount of trauma, including seeing the traumatic situations of other people, so I don't think looking away helps, but knowing your limits definitely does.

You also need to understand how news agencies have worked for centuries: the more trash they bring to the attention of listeners, viewers and readers, the larger the audience they get. If you read 100-year-old newspapers, it's about the end of the world and humans experiencing suffering. Bringing attention to these issues is necessary to resolve them, but drama doesn't help the people who actually work on that (ask me how I know).

The Middle East has had different types of conflicts; they are centuries old, and life is not enough to study even one of them in its complexity. But life is enough to watch the "Fauda" series, and it's definitely worth it.

It's about understanding your limits, what you can face, understand or change. And I think doing something locally to the best of your abilities is the best way to change the world in the best possible way, but there is a catch. Being in a war zone isn't for civilians, so if you are there, just get out first.

Structural crises

There's a structural crisis going on, probably several of them simultaneously. Mixing them with other unfortunate events doesn't help, but increases anxiety. By structural crisis, I mean the IT/AI crisis, but I believe that every crisis opens new opportunities. Some old opportunities are closing, and being stubborn and following the old path doesn't help.

Let's look at it from another angle: if you are in a startup environment, you'll hear the word "disruptive" in a positive sense. The new companies should disrupt old businesses by bringing substantially more value and offering cheaper goods and services. It's nice to use the fruits of these disruptive changes, but living in this time is rough, especially if your job is the one being made obsolete.

And let's go one step further: I've seen businesses, business models or even industries that should be disrupted. They look disgusting inside because they don't care about the value they bring, they do not know who their customers are and they have forgotten about costs completely. Sometimes this can't be cured, and it takes more time to go bankrupt when the company has a pile of cash.

Let's get to the measures to live with the crises:

  • Adapt, there's no way around it.
  • Choose between official courses and self-study consciously, because "official" doesn't guarantee anything.
  • Move faster, experiment, check the facts.

Jobs

Job search takes its toll on everyone: depreciated effort, ego being humiliated, dealing with incompetence and discrimination. The question is even how to get to the people who are still able to listen and choose reasonably. I assume that everyone gets a chance by putting enough effort into it. But let's assume you just finished a credible institute and you have to compete with a 40-50-year-old fart like me. Let's imagine you are sitting in the same room and you have a chance to persuade the employer to choose you – what will you say?

  • Working more? What I've seen, people providing for a family don't lack motivation.
  • Learning faster? Some people are stuck, but don't underestimate others; people can learn.
  • Being friendlier or playing the "work relations" card in some other way? I've seen a lot of people doing it.

I think you need a plan. Some particular points of it could be the following:

  • Taking a job in a remote location; the competition for these jobs can be dramatically lower, and you'll get the experience you need. Married people are usually tied to places.
  • Having a particular suggestions to substitute the old tech stack. People are afraid to have suggestions, and a person with a wrong suggestion can still win over a person with no suggestions.
  • Digging deeper into the basics: business, process modeling, anything. I've seen a lot of people who have only superficial knowledge, and they are not ready for a discussion. And the management knows it; they just don't have anyone to choose from.

Inputs

Our minds and bodies run the processes, and only the processes are important at the end of the day. You've probably heard of "Atomic Habits", and that's what forms the processes. What I mean by processes is that our minds and bodies transform inputs into outputs. It's extremely important to watch the inputs:

  • What food we digest
  • What information you consume
  • How much and how well you sleep; it's an input as well, and it helps your mind and body to recover
  • Do you challenge your mind with tasks?
  • Do you stimulate your body with physical exercises?
  • Do you have spiritual development?

The Greeks, in their wisdom, invented and described all this long ago, as well as critical thinking and rules of discussion. And these basics still allow people to win. It's now just packaged as energy management or mood management. I was surprised how important it actually is for me to listen to the good old songs in the morning and how important the preparation-for-sleep routine turned out to be. And I read exactly one source of information regarding politics, just to stay sane.

Conclusions

With my parents, I remember the exact point in time when I realized that their life experience was no longer relevant and I shouldn't listen to their advice. Maybe my advice is outdated as well – if so, I'd vote for critical analysis of the information in this post above everything else.

This moment was liberating in some ways, as well as making me feel the full load of responsibility for my life and the lives of those depending on me. What I regret most is that, with the current turbulence, boys and girls are experiencing this moment when they are not ready yet; they are not tough enough. The psyche can crack under this load, and you can see it's happening almost online. And those who choose violent protests are not going to listen; they believe that there's an easy fix.

Anyway, everything's gonna be alright. ©

entry.title: A Protected Static Website with Caddy and Pocket ID
entry.content:
Intro

In the Intranet post we talked about using just a static website, and there's a stigma here. If you ask any IT specialist "How do I get a protected static website?", they'll tell you to get a VPN. Which is at least overcomplicated.

The second stigma is that you need different password to access every resource, although auth services, one of which is Pocket ID, are available and are not that complicated. Yes, you definitely can and should have a single authentication system for all your services, because it's convenient and safer. Every time a user types in a password, it's actually bad from a security viewpoint.

And there's a third common misconception, which actually made me write this post: you need more than a web server and an auth service to protect a static website. The reason is that an auth service usually expects an application to handle the authentication flow and communicate with it. A static website doesn't do that: it simply serves files and has no backend or authentication endpoints. This is where a reverse proxy comes in: it handles the authentication flow with the auth service and only serves the website to authenticated users. But with Caddy (a webserver) you can get a reverse proxy as well.

I'd briefly describe how I set up a web server (Caddy) and an auth service (Pocket ID) for a static website, as it required some debugging. Both products I used are written in Go, which gives you a few advantages right away:

  • Small resource footprint
  • Fast and scalable, especially with more requests
  • It's a single binary, so you can use Docker, but you can install it on bare metal as well

Config

The whole process is as follows:

  1. Add records to hosts.conf to point to app.local.lan (the website) and auth.local.lan (the auth service)
  2. Install Caddy (probably bare metal) and Pocket ID, probably with Docker
  3. Install a security module for Caddy, which can integrate a static website with Pocket ID
  4. Configure Pocket ID: two lines in the config file and a few steps in a web interface
  5. Add lines to Caddy's config

I found Pocket ID configuration easy, but here are the steps for reference:

  1. You add a client
  2. You add a user group
  3. You give this user group access to the client

Any chatbot or documentation can guide you, but every chatbot I tested starts going in circles with Caddy's config, as the security module config is not so obvious. So here it is:

{
#    debug
	security {
		oauth identity provider generic {
			delay_start 3
			realm generic
			driver generic
			client_id <your client id created in Pocket ID>
			client_secret <your client secret created in Pocket ID>
			scopes openid email profile

			base_auth_url https://auth.local.lan
			metadata_url http://127.0.0.1:1411/.well-known/openid-configuration
		}

		authentication portal my_portal {
			enable identity provider generic
			cookie insecure off

			trust login redirect uri domain exact app.local.lan path prefix /

			transform user {
				match realm generic
				action add role authp/user
			}
		}

		authorization policy my_policy {
			set auth url /caddy-security/oauth2/generic
			allow roles authp/user
		}
	}
}

app.local.lan {
	tls internal

	@portal path /caddy-security/*
	route @portal {
		authenticate with my_portal
	}

	route {
		authorize with my_policy
		root * /var/www/html
		file_server
	}
}

auth.local.lan {
	tls internal
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:1411
}

Beware, this is for localhost only, so it doesn't use real SSL certificates, which Caddy can easily install for you.

Caddy is really nice:

  1. It has a validation tool to tell you about the errors in your config.
  2. It has a formatting tool to fix the issues.
  3. It has a debug mode (uncomment in the beginning) and you can check the logs to troubleshoot any issues.

Conclusion

I guess the main outcome is that everyone needs to be challenged, even your friendly IT colleagues, and pushed to use the modern tech stack, especially if it cuts costs dramatically.

entry.title: Gaming Review on Linux No One Asked For
entry.content:
Disclaimer: the hardware market is experiencing a price surge. Common sense, statistics, history and economics tell us that crises pass and commodity prices go down, so the recommendation for now is to wait, at least until January.

Intro

It's December again, time to play Helldivers 2 with the boys – or so I thought. The reality is that Arrowhead changed the anti-cheat for the game, so although it probably works better on Linux (no official support though), it doesn't work with cloud gaming anymore, except for Xbox Cloud. What are the options?

  • A tinkering project with AMD BC-250
  • A gaming PC
  • Surprisingly, a console

AMD BC-250

Aside from all the crises, AMD BC-250 costing less than 100 bucks became overhyped after some videos on YouTube, and it's really a thing: enough power, really cheap, and you can unlock even more cores. So, you'll need a power supply, a case (which can be 3D-printed, so even more fun here) and fans. Plenty of tinkering, it mostly works, plenty of customization options, well documented. It really surprised me how the Linux gaming community has grown over the years, because to use this very specific hardware you'll need Linux, and here are the options:

  • CachyOS, which is Arch-based and optimized best for this hardware.
  • SteamOS, which is also Arch-based
  • Bazzite, which is Fedora-based, but immutable
  • Fedora, which is a major Linux distribution

You can install Steam on all of these distros, and Steam installs games for a particular user, so no difference here.

Arch is not my weapon of choice (I'm not a virgin anymore, you know), as well as immutable distributions, so I'd probably stay with Fedora, which I used for years before Debian (Debian sucked then). As Fedora is a normal distribution, you'll be able to simply install the software (it's more complicated with immutable distros) and use it like a normal computer for any tasks you want. And what do you want from a gaming PC? Well, you'd probably want to run a local LLM, and there's a catch here. With AMD, you'd probably want AMD ROCm, which is like Nvidia CUDA and which is not (yet fully) supported here.

Gaming PC

Well, I want a local LLM, and I'll get a gaming PC to run it, as well as games. It's not that simple:

  • Nvidia CUDA is a great tech, but Nvidia on Linux is the same pain in the butt it always was, because of the closed-source drivers
  • AMD GPU would be an obvious choice, but AMD ROCm is supported by a lot fewer cards than you'd expect, so you need to check carefully before you buy

Why do we discuss LLMs if we started with gaming PCs? Well, we can get more value from LLMs out of the same hardware, which can justify the price. For almost any other software, even video editing (which can also be done in the cloud or with AI in the cloud) can be accomplished now with an integrated video card, which is... an overlooked piece of good news, I guess?

So, taking into account the power consumption (which can get up to 1kW or more) of a gaming PC, the question is probably: do I really need one? When I look at all these LEDs, it makes me sad, because I'm far past the age when colourful LEDs could bring joy. So, if you are still with me, the question actually remains: are there any other options? And a console can be the answer.

Console

If you understand the hardware and software just a little bit, you get the main hardship with software performance optimization: with standard software, it's 1; with the whole software zoo, it's N. Consoles are pieces of hardware which are well tested, cheap and the software is optimized for them. A side note: this could be the actual reason to make a Steam Machine. The main players are Sony with PlayStation and Microsoft with Xbox (oh, and Valve with Steam Deck and Steam Machine). Xbox is cheaper. To play games over the network, you also need to pay monthly for the service, but you get a bunch of games to play.

With my HD2 situation, there's no cross-progression, so all my achievements stay on my PC account, and there's no mouse and keyboard, which is depressing. And you need to buy another copy of the game for Xbox. There's cloud gaming, which technically should work in Chrome on Linux, but you'll need a controller anyway, because it's an Xbox in the cloud and it expects to see a controller, as well as a copy of the game.

Can you repurpose your game console for anything else? The answer is no with PlayStation and Xbox and yes with Steam Machine, as it's a normal Linux PC. The price of the Steam Machine is harder to justify though, as it's the most expensive of all.

Conclusion

I define progress as something being faster and more accessible (cheaper), so we're kind of going back and forth here: we have cloud gaming for Linux, but it doesn't work in my particular case anymore. It's always a limited number of games, by the way, unless you rent a physical gaming Windows PC. We have Steam Machine, but it's pricey, like 2x compared to Xbox. We always had AMD and Nvidia options for graphics and benefited as consumers from their competition; now we get technologies for running LLMs locally, but Nvidia with closed Linux drivers and AMD with lacking ROCm support kind of hold us back. The progress of supporting Windows games on Linux is astonishing though, largely thanks to Valve. But it's always this feeling that gamers are some stupid human beings who will justify any price and any restricting conditions.

entry.title: Educational Videos Are Still Worth It
entry.content:
Intro

I personally use YouTube largely as an educational resource, and it makes me sad to see some YouTubers abandoning their channels, blaming AI, lower attention spans and structural crises. I'm a fan of educational videos, although it's better to try and hack it yourself, as well as read the manual. What's so special about educational videos?

  • You can find a video that explains the solution the way you like it (or when the author struggles with exactly the same issue you face)
  • It's about trust: you see the solution actually working, you can see all the steps that lead to it, and you start to believe that you can do it too
  • It's asynchronous: you can find the time that suits you best; it may be 2am, when you can watch it, pause or watch again some moments that are important

I'm working in a B2B/IT context, and it's specific for a number of reasons. It's restrictive in terms of software, format or the goals the videos should achieve. At the same time, I find a space for creativity inside these restrictive boundaries, and I'd like to tell you my way of solving this problem: recording a video that actually helps someone.

Preparation

Well, you can start recording right away, but you'll learn quickly that preparation is key. In an IT context, the programs and settings should work, so there's no room for errors or even warnings. The last time I was doing it, it took me 10 tries to set up the data in the ERP system, figure out the right sequence of actions and get comfortable with this logic myself. But I don't rely on my memory alone!

So the next step is to write down the script. You can treat it as a guideline, feeling free to deviate from it, or even use a mind map just for the structure, but I prefer the full text, as it reveals inconsistencies early on. The next step is to read the script out loud, to make sure it sounds good and you are comfortable with it. You'd probably want to read it a few more times to remember the scenario.

There are a few life hacks to calm down if you feel too much pressure or anxiety: meditate and breathe, or close your eyes and play the whole recording session in your head beforehand. I allow my anxiety to kick in this time, so the situation will be familiar to the brain, and it will think, "Oh, I've been there, so nothing happened," and it will calm down.

Recording

I prefer to split the recording sessions into 2-3 minute chunks, to glue them together afterwards (which is a simple operation for the computer, by the way), and you'll be able to go relatively fast through one chunk, then take a break. Some important points of recording operations with software:

  • Try to start exactly where you finished the last chunk; I try even not to move the mouse.
  • Don't split the logical operations that should finish successfully from beginning to end; it will show up and you'll just confuse yourself.
  • You can record several times, but in some cases you'll need to change the data or start from the beginning (regrettably): for instance, your viewers need to see that the production orders are derived from the production plan you worked with before.

The tech side of the effort is the software. If you have an opportunity to install OBS Studio, just go for it. If you are in a restricted Windows environment, surprisingly, you can use the infamous Snipping Tool to record the screencast and the audio, and it works. If you need a video from your camera in the corner, go for OBS Studio. If you prefer to record audio afterwards, I'd not recommend that. It always seemed strange, and you'll need a video editor (one more program).

Making a product

To glue the things together, you'd need ffmpeg, which is a command-line utility available for Mac, Linux and Windows. I used it in WSL for obvious reasons; it works just fine.

The first thing to do is to glue the files together, and ffmpeg does it without re-encoding if the encodings of all the files match. As input, you feed ffmpeg a list of files in a particular order (Captain Obvious here), and you get a single file.

The second step is to compress the video (with ffmpeg as well); I'd just use a chatbot to get the proper command-line parameters. In my case, it compressed a 1.2 GB video to 42 MB, which made it a lot easier to distribute without any quality loss! Again, compressing your video with the right parameters is respecting your viewers. And you never know how many views you'll get!

Conclusion

Nothing new here: preparation is key. And having a plan like "How am I going to edit the video?" helps with the technical issues. I did some video editing; the issue here is that it's a time-consuming and resource-consuming process. Some people enjoy it; you can apply effects and transitions, but it takes about 6x the recording time. I just have some stuff to do. :) If a lack of time or video-editing skills prevents you from sharing information with the world or your colleagues, now you have a recipe, I hope.

entry.title: We Need More Web Terminals
entry.content:
Intro

So it was a Friday afternoon, and I found myself working on my computer locally as well as having 3 remote desktop sessions open, one of which was in a different domain, and I was trying to figure out how to copy a file between domains. So I opened Explorer as a user from a different domain, but as long as these machines didn't share any resources, it didn't help. And I thought to myself: it shouldn't be that complicated, although each and every step of how we got into this situation was logical. I also thought that the UX was far from smooth: some remote sessions required logging in, some didn't, it was hard to switch between them, and overall I found 4 desktops kind of overwhelming for me, one human being. I feel overwhelmed with more than 10 open tabs in the browser, and if you click on any link in any session, you get a new browser window in each session. That's rough.

Pros

Web technologies made their way into all types of apps, including the most conservative ones, the ERP systems. The front-end frameworks matured, easing development and taking away the complexity of testing your app for each browser. And the browsers matured as well. And it came to the point where I don't get why the app is not web-based, as long as it's not a legacy one:

  • You get an application server "for free", and this 3-tier architecture is probably the best way to balance the load and process the data between the database and the application server. If you didn't understand the previous sentence, don't worry, it was something specific to my MS Dynamics AX implementation experience, because the devs of this system invented their own application server.
  • It's safe, fast enough, and you get a remote option for free: you can work with your app remotely without a VPN. And the VPN experience is also, by the way, far from smooth, as long as you need to use the Internet as well.
  • It's easy on the users, because modern front-end frameworks incorporate the UX we need, and the UX people have got used to when browsing websites. It's exactly the case where standards work, and it saves people lots of hours, because they don't have to figure out how to interact with the app.

The options

And thinking about all this, I came across ChromeOS Flex, an operating system with a browser intended for launching web apps, as well as Cameyo, a way to deliver Windows apps to this desktop as web apps. It surprised me that this technology already exists, and that it's not recommended only for graphics-heavy apps. It all costs money: you need to pay to administer ChromeOS Flex desktops, and you also need to pay for the server software. Is there another way?

I thought of "a poor man's web terminal" as a Debian desktop with Chrome or Chromium. You'll probably have two types of users: "power users", being able to learn and use the power of the Linux environment and native apps (like ffmpeg, for example), their speciality being dealing with non-standard tasks. And it's kind of strange (and counterproductive) to restrict their environment to the browser only. On the other hand, you'll have people working with a pre-defined set of apps, and for them, one local app, the browser, could probably be enough, provided your apps are web-based. You could even take it one step further by booting these desktops over the network and mounting their home folders on the server, minimizing the maintenance time and cost.

A lean server setup

For a small company, I'd start with the following set of web apps:

  • E-mail, you need it in the cloud. With both Google and Microsoft, you get a web email client by default, and you don't get any friction from administering your own email server.
  • It's a good question whether you should use Google's or Microsoft's office web apps. I find them both underpowered. You'd probably want to have some file exchange, and here you have another question: whether you should trust your files to these US companies. All that being said, I'd go with ownCloud, which has several office connectors, and some office products can work as web apps on the client but can also be installed on your server.
  • I'd go for some web-based task manager (my favourite at the time being Gitea) for general admin tasks, it-support tasks and specific projects.
  • I'd go for a statically generated website for an intranet. And yes, I think if you can't figure out how to use a static site generator, you probably shouldn't post your thoughts on the website. :)
  • For any other apps, I'd search for Go alternatives first, because they are simple to install, they imply the right backend logic, and they consume a lot fewer resources than other apps (especially Java ones).

All these choices give us even more reasons to use web terminals, or a computer with a browser as the main app, or an app-launching platform.

Conclusions

It's funny to find that someone already monetises the thing that buzzes you, but I'm generally optimistic about progress: as long as this solution or architecture reveals its advantages, free and open-source alternatives will emerge. In fact, they already exist, with Cameyo cutting resource consumption and costs even more by providing only the required applications, not the whole desktop. And I quietly wait for someone to say that the Windows desktop experience has become unacceptable. Today I had a bad experience with a mouse moving as if the computer were under heavy load, although it wasn't. And I wouldn't be surprised if I found out that guys at Microsoft were using Linux desktops whenever they could, because it's just so much better. And yes, I have made peace with Debian.

entry.title: Playing Football Is By Far the Best Experience of This Year
entry.content:
How it started

It started with muscle cramps after the first touch of the ball, literally. I tried to massage my leg, but it didn't help, so I had to leave. The second time, both Achilles tendons hurt, and I had to skip about a month. Trying to run tended to worsen the situation, and it hurts now every time until I warm up. But you know what? Somehow YouTube showed me a video of a woman in yoga leggings recommending stretching the Achilles tendons, and the caption said something like "you are sitting the whole day, what do you want from your body?" So it seems to be a me-problem, and if a simple 10-minute-a-day stretch can fix it, there's just nothing to talk about. In the meantime, I discovered a warm-up routine from some English gentleman and advice from the chatbot regarding the training runs. So now I run not by distance, but by time, for about 20 minutes. And it seems that the human body was designed to regularly take some load just to feel normal, but a body needs to sweat. I feel a lot better after each training session, physically and mentally, but playing football brings something very special too.

Being with the boys

I think socializing is underappreciated. And my friends laugh when I tell them that men are somewhat psychologically wired to need to be among other men. We don't discuss a lot, because we come to play football, but I like these guys, and although they don't know it, they somehow helped me navigate through a rough period of my life. I kind of lost the thread of what is normal, what human and manlike reactions are, how you should normally react to small talk, uncomfortable situations or conflicts (don't ask how it happened).

I don't drink beer, I don't talk about my background, but they somehow learned to read my emotions, and the funniest part is that my emotions matter to them. And yes, cultural difference is a thing, and I stepped right on it in one case, but that's how I learned something valuable. To me, it seemed like excessive bureaucracy, which I hate, and to them, it was the system that just works, so there's no need to change it. And playing football after work requires understanding (sometimes guessing) German words quickly, and that even doesn't count as a challenge.

The challenges

They warned me from the start that they participate in the championship. I was just like, "I'm fine with it". But an official game, even in the lowest league with no spectators, is a completely different experience compared to training, and it motivates you to progress and to give it your all. But the first challenge was to get to that game, because it was usually a new location, which I needed to find in time.

The second challenge was bringing beer or washing the uniform for the team. There's also some more logistics involved if you have a car and want to help someone get to the game in time, and I also learned about the "traditions" (where we meet) the hard way, but look, I didn't screw up for a long time, and it was kind of revealing to me. Beer is actually the most challenging, because you have to buy it, bring it home and cool it down, and then not forget to bring it to the game. One mistake and the team gets warm beer or no beer, and you see at least 10 disappointed guys, which is really motivating not to do it the next time.

How it ended

Oh, I'm not done with playing football, but the season ended. And I'd like to tell you how the last game of the season went. So we had a training session with the guys from the upper league. They all seemed to be former pros, they all ran fast, had good technique, and when they split the team, I played with these guys. So I lost all the balls I got, couldn't get to the ball because I wasn't fast enough, couldn't score a goal – I couldn't do almost anything, although I gave it my all. But I remember vividly how I played and how I felt in February – like a bag full of shit, and I couldn't run at all. The improvement in less than a year was huge for me, and I keep smiling when I remember that game. And it was positive overall; everyone was relaxed and just enjoyed the game. There are some social mechanics involved, like calibrating myself, and I'm starting to think, maybe I shouldn't be that hard on myself. And, playing twice a week and running once a week, I lost some weight effortlessly. That alone was kind of amazing.

entry.title: CNC: Calendar, Notes, Commitment
entry.content:
Notes

You actually start with a brainstorming phase, and that's when it's important to write down all the ideas: to get them out of your head, not to let them bother you anymore, to free your head for new ideas and to have a place to elaborate on ideas a little bit further. I use Google Keep, because it's really smart about syncing stuff across the devices, but any note-taking app will fit, as long as you have your phone nearby. Maybe you have a paperback notebook, then it will do too, but it should be effortless to find this note-taking device and to write things down, because some things tend not to come the second time.

I prefer to make hierarchical lists, because they allow me to move points up and down (whatever that means), make levels connect meaning, delete them all at once or mark them as completed. All the brainstorming rules apply: no critique, write down any idea that comes along, look at the ideas the next day and so on. That's how most of my blog posts start, by the way.

Calendar

Some things in the notes are action items, but to become such, sometimes they need the time and place, and that's where a calendar comes in handy. Any calendar will do, as long as it has these features:

  • It is synced across the devices, so you have exactly one place to look for your plans.
  • It supports time zones in case you have meetings with people from different time zones.
  • It has notifications; sometimes I need 10 minutes before the event, sometimes 30 minutes and sometimes 1 hour.

The difference between the notes and the calendar is the decision to spend your time doing something, and it's called a commitment. So we'll talk about commitment a little bit.

Commitment

Relations come to my mind first when I hear the expression "a lack of commitment". And yes, one approach to evaluating the importance (of commitment, in this case) is to imagine exactly the same circumstances but without this one thing: what difference do you see? I'm not an expert in relations in any way, maybe some people just meet their ideal ones and get happy, but I've seen couples splitting while sharing the same values (which is important), with one of these values being... a lack of commitment. No one can explain what's happening; it's not some fight or hardships, people just fail to commit. Of course I speak about romantic relations, but I see the same stuff with friendships or partnerships, especially if it's some hobby. If you plan something, just ask someone to send an invitation to a calendar or offer to send it yourself. If people look at you like a psycho, there are a few options here:

  • You are a psycho, probably not diagnosed yet, just like me.
  • People are not ready to commit to this extent – to the extent of the meeting in the calendar.

I try to have all the important events in my calendar for some not-so-obvious reasons, other than not forgetting about them:

  • Not to commit to something else at the same time
  • Not to mess up with the time zones (see the section "Calendar" above)
  • Not to get into discussions about "who said what" after the meeting didn't happen

It's beyond the scope of this post to discuss how stressful life is and whether we are overcommitted in general (probably we are, on average), but every time I see a person having difficulties committing to something, exactly one question pops out in my mind: am I talking to an adult? I don't say being an adult is easy, but making commitments, breaking them and feeling the consequences, from my perspective, is what being an adult means. Like you are supposed to take this amount of frustration, which, by the way, as my therapist framed it, contributes to your personal growth. And I feel bad for people failing to commit, because they rob themselves of personal growth – kind of an easy way to live, I get it, but I don't buy it.

Conclusion

I assume challenging yourself is the most important condition for long-term survival, and I challenge myself and fail when nobody sees it. The most frequent case being: writing a few thoughts for a blog post and failing to write the post. There are two types of posts: concrete and abstract, just like this one. It's hard to get the relevant stories, it's hard to get the arguments pro and contra, it's kind of hard to figure out what I'm thinking about all this, so I fail again and again.

And I think about kids, who fail at school again and again, and that's the only way to learn. My daughter told me they have discussions at school and that the first time they fail, including jumping to other subjects and failing to lead a civilized discussion overall. And the topic doesn't matter, even if it seems there's little room for discussion there. We think that school is an exercise and adult life is about accomplishing everything successfully the first time, but it doesn't work this way. I think it's all an exercise, but when you fail, you get better.

entry.title: Messing Around With Audio
entry.content:
How it started

So I had the following audio setup:

Alexa ----(Bluetooth)---+
                        +--> Speakers
Computer --(Bluetooth)--+
   +<--(USB)-- Mic
   +--(3.5mm jack)--> Headphones

And I had the following use cases:

  1. Listening to music from Spotify
  2. Watching movies (on the computer)
  3. Video calls & podcasts

And I thought: the third part just works, and I'm happy with that. But maybe I could improve the setup for music & movies, because wired connections, wired speakers, and decent acoustics could make a difference. By the way, if you didn't know it, Alexa can connect to and disconnect from the Bluetooth speaker using voice commands. And it acts as a Spotify device, so I can control it from my phone using the Spotify app, which makes it quite useful.

The Raspberry Pi part

There are some special devices for listening to Spotify. They receive a network connection (probably, Wi-Fi) and have an output for the speakers. But if you add the movie-watching scenario to this, not all speakers are capable of switching sources, so you can end up needing a special device for that, which is suboptimal, to say the least. I thought: what's the state of computer audio for Raspberry Pi (RaPi), as it could be a good fit? And that's what I've found:

  1. You can have any RaPi you want, including the Zero 2 W, and use Raspotify to play music and control RaPi with your phone or computer.
  2. If you want to play a movie and transmit audio to RaPi, you can do it with PulseAudio (a Linux audio system), but you'll get a delay over Wi-Fi. Adding Ethernet, which is required (but I haven't tested it, and there's still a chance you'll get a delay), adds complexity and requires a USB-to-Ethernet adapter, so you end up with a RaPi 3B+ and a HiFi HAT (a board for audio output).
  3. A HiFi HAT can have a DAC (which stands for digital-to-analog converter), so you can connect it to the speakers via RCA (analog) cables, or you can have an optical output, but you'll need another DAC: either an external one or one integrated into the speakers.
Computer --(Ethernet)--> RaPi --(RCA)--> Speakers

or

Computer --(Ethernet)--> RaPi --(Optical)--> DAC --(RCA)--> Speakers

Could you hear the difference between digital and analog cables? Probably not. Could you hear the difference between an external DAC and one integrated into decent speakers? Probably not. But both options are better than transmitting analog audio from the computer, because the computer's DAC can be worse and the computer can add noise to the analog signal.

RaPi is a side quest because it has a lot of use cases. Could I run an NFS server with a USB HDD? It would work, but for better performance, you'd need a RaPi 4, ideally with an SSD HAT and an SSD for the operating system. So the budget here can grow rapidly, although you could repurpose RaPi for other projects in the future. Another thing to note is that the speakers need a power supply, and RaPi needs one too, but a DAC can work just fine with a USB-C connection to the computer for both audio and power.

How would RaPi switch between the audio sources (computer / Spotify)? It should work fine with PulseAudio, but by default it will mix the channels.

Does an external DAC have any advantages? Yes, kind of: it can make your headphones sound better if they're high-quality ones. It also has a volume knob. It can convert an analog signal from the mic with less distortion than a computer, but I have a mic with an ADC built in, so it's better to connect the mic directly to the PC via USB in this case.

Hybrid variants are also possible: leave RaPi Zero 2 W (Wi-Fi) alone with Spotify and connect it via RCA to the speakers. Then connect the computer to the speakers via optical cable, and switch the sources on the speakers. Then you can listen to music without turning on your computer, which probably saves some energy, but I think a laptop is quite efficient.

RaPi Zero 2 W --(RCA)--+
                       +--> Speakers
Computer ---(Optical)--+

The PC part

At this point, I thought: do I need a RaPi? It won't give me voice commands, it requires a power supply and a separate budget, and I can do the same with the PC, which I don't turn off; it just sleeps when not in use. And I can control Spotify on the PC remotely with my phone; it's just another Spotify device. The PC is the only sound source, so all I need is a USB-to-optical converter because the speakers do not have a USB port.

How it ended

I haven't decided yet. From a minimalist standpoint, the speakers + PC setup looks favorable, and I don't have to deal with all this RaPi architecture. Switching between outputs on the PC also looks convenient. Good speakers take up some space, though, and I kind of like my cable-free, voice-controlled setup. But better speakers and a wired connection should make a difference for music.

As you probably noticed, I haven't considered soundbars because modern speakers have source switching and all the same input options, and stereo music sounds better. Soundbars occupy a niche for TVs, and they sound accordingly, especially with action movies. It still feels like some devices lack inputs, audio interfaces, or source switches, and you have to think too much about how to combine all this into a working system. It's kind of disappointing.

entry.title: Working CV Is About Consistency
entry.content:
Intro

Looking for a job can be so challenging that it takes a mental toll on us, and we tend to avoid this irritating task of reviewing and editing the CV one more time. Even when we read the CV, it can be overwhelming to stick to the goals. And the CV has only one goal – to get you in the door, or, in other words, to get you to the first interview round, which is usually with HR. HR people don't know anything about your job, especially if you are well qualified in your field – so well that it's hard for anyone outside your field to understand what you are actually doing. So HR people tend to concentrate on the 10% of the CV they can understand and whether the overall picture is taking shape:

  1. What was your career path?
  2. What did you achieve and what were you actually paid for?
  3. What do you do well and want to do in your next job?

These are tough questions, as your career path can be non-linear, with movements back and forth, career breaks for many different reasons, and jobs you did well but are no longer willing to do. Well, I don't have the statistics on hand, but I think this is a common case, so the task here is to make it look linear, even if it isn't. Why linear? Well, human beings follow linear stories best, and your CV is your story. Your next job should look like a logical next chapter of this story. And storytelling is hard, make no mistake about that. Stories that only scratch the surface don't touch anyone, so this should be a story about how you found your passion and followed it despite all the obstacles. Mistakes along the way are actually advantages because they mean you risked something, gained experience, and are persistent enough to follow your path further. I would hire a person like that. Let's start from the inside.

Finding your passion

First, there are a lot of great books on the topic, and if the tip below doesn't do you any good, just go out there and find some information. The only thing I'm sure about is that you shouldn't approach work without passion, because passion indicates that you have high expectations and are ready to invest your time and energy to get what you expect – so you're just waiting for the tasks. And my tip would probably work best for people with some work experience. For students and schoolkids, I'd definitely recommend getting some experience; the best time is probably a year after finishing school. But let's get back on track.

So, here's the story. It was an interview at a mining company with an almost nonexistent project culture (in terms of business transformation) and some red flags regarding the internal atmosphere. But it was a functioning business anyway, and they somehow managed to get some stuff done on a large scale. And the manager asked me this question: Who are you? I was surprised by this direct question, and it made me reply without questioning myself: I'm a consultant. I had worked as a consultant before and felt emotionally and professionally in the right place in that role. The point was that they didn't have consultants; they had managers who took full responsibility, so I obviously didn't fit. If your answer is "I don't know", that's fine, as long as you're passionately looking for your place in life, the place where you bring value to society and are happy about it. In a case I saw recently, three different roles were mixed in one CV, and obviously, only one of them reflected that person's passion. Just ask yourself.

Cutting the excess

I assume that a CV is a 100% functional document: it should get you in the door; that's its only function. It works or it's worthless, and people tend to forget about that. It's not a monument to your life, it's not about describing all the experiences you've had, and it's not about showing the world what a multifaceted person you are. It doesn't need to look nice or smart, so if you're hesitating over whether it makes sense to edit your latest "holy" version, which you like so much, just ask yourself: Did it get you interviews? If it didn't, edit it now.

Obviously, you need to match your skill set and experience with the positions on the market, and I know exactly two approaches that work here. The first is resource-consuming, and you need some skills to do market research. So you analyze the open positions, probably the economic situation as well, to calculate your chances. Then you tailor your CV to target a particular segment and go for it. At this stage, you probably know the words used in job titles and descriptions, and that's a serious advantage. The second approach is hypothesis testing: you say, "This job probably exists, and I could do it." It seems that the chances of guessing correctly are low, but I prefer this method because I get feedback quickly and collect valuable information. You probably won't succeed in the first iteration, but the information you get will allow you to tailor your CV faster.

And tailoring is the key word here. It means cutting everything that distracts attention from your target role. I compressed the first five years of my career, during which I worked at different companies and completed very challenging projects, into one sentence because otherwise I got only roles as a Microsoft Dynamics consultant, and I had decided to go into management consulting. It's hard to overcome the emotional attachment to those years of my career, but in that case, it was worth it, and I got what I wanted. Bonus tip: it allowed me to cut my CV to one page, and I got more interviews because HR people were kind of intrigued by this short version.

Making it consistent

A very special HR tip is that HR people are just normal people reading your CV, so they can't understand your highly specialized professional stuff, but they can understand inconsistencies that any human being can spot:

  • Jumping between manager, sales, and specialist roles
  • Mixing what you delivered (the business results) with the process that led to it
  • Having more than three bullet points for each role

You see, I could write about many more inconsistencies, but I chose the three most important ones because there's a magic trick behind the way people process information in series of three. An inconsistency can also reveal itself in how you write about different positions: if some of them are described in more detail, you're probably hiding something about the others. And if the style is different (the language, the rhythm, even the grammar), you simply haven't done your homework and haven't read the CV yourself to make it consistent. It's just about respecting the other party, the reader: they shouldn't have any difficulties reading your CV from beginning to end. Nothing should stick out or catch their attention if it shouldn't. Just pretend for a moment that you're the reader and read it one more time. Mark all the inconsistencies ruthlessly, then take one more iteration to correct them. For some psychological reason, a printed CV works better for this exercise because you don't switch to "editing" mode immediately.

Making it work

That wasn't easy, but that's not all there is to it. The hardest part is this: if it were your job to hire this person, would you do it? If the answer is no, you probably need some more iterations. But if you just send your CV "as is", you close the doors (the opportunities) yourself, because you can send your CV only once. There is some reasoning behind people just spamming others with their CV: it's better than doing nothing, I'll be noticed at least – and so on. But "at least" is not enough. You either get the attention you need to be invited to an interview, or you don't. Many things can go wrong, starting with the CV format, the words you use, or the job market, but, all other things being equal, I'd hire a person who acts reasonably in a stressful situation over a person who goes into full panic mode. I'd actually prefer a reasonable person with a huge handicap in skills and experience. There was a reason to put "Don't Panic" on the cover of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, you know.

Conclusions

If I were to write a history of the present time, I'd describe it as a time of transition, and it's the hardest time to live in (probably not that hard compared to times without the Internet and toilet paper). We are stressed because we know something has changed, but we don't know how to adapt, or adapting is too painful: it seems that you need some black magic to satisfy LinkedIn algorithms and AI, which won't let your CV reach a human. And I just don't buy it: if a company can't choose a functioning AI, I don't want to work for that company, because they have probably made some other bad management decisions. The same goes for using strange LinkedIn features or hiring unprofessional HR people. How do I deal with this craziness? I deal only with reasonable people. My motto is: if the world goes crazy, it doesn't mean I have to. But communicating your strengths to sentient people is important and worth investing some effort in, from my perspective. I also assume that the percentage of craziness is constant; it's just more visible now.
